desc:
A chess king stands on the top-left cell of a rectangular board. Cells with 1 are blocked, cells with 0 are free. In one move the king goes to any of the up to 8 neighbouring cells (horizontally, vertically or diagonally adjacent) that lie on the board and are free. The king may revisit cells.

Return the number of different move sequences of exactly k moves that end on the bottom-right cell, modulo 1,000,000,007. Two sequences differ if the lists of visited cells differ. If the start or the destination is blocked the answer is 0.

board = 2x2 all free   k = 1 -> 1,  k = 2 -> 2,  k = 3 -> 7
board = [[0,1],[1,0]], k = 2 -> 0

With k = 0 the king does not move, so the answer is 1 only when the board has a single free cell, and 0 otherwise.
hints: Walks may revisit cells, so there is no 'visited' set. What matters about a partial walk is only where it currently stands and how many moves are left.
Let f[t][r][c] be the number of walks of exactly t moves that start at the top-left and end at (r, c).
f[t][r][c] is the sum of f[t-1] over the free neighbours of (r, c) (up to 8 of them), with f[0] equal to 1 at the start and 0 elsewhere. Only the previous layer is needed.
editorial: A walk of t moves ending at a free cell has a last move from one of its neighbouring free cells, after a walk of t-1 moves. That gives the recurrence f[t][r][c] = sum of f[t-1][r'][c'] over the 8 neighbours (r', c') that are inside the board and free, and f is 0 on blocked cells. Layer 0 has a single 1 on the start cell. After k layers the answer is f[k] at the bottom-right cell.

Since layer t only reads layer t-1, two m × n arrays are enough. The work is k · m · n · 8 additions, tiny for this input size. Reduce modulo 1,000,000,007 after each layer. The recurrence is exactly 'multiply by the adjacency matrix of the king graph k times', which is why a much larger k would call for matrix exponentiation.
